A **unital associative superalgebra over $\mathbb C$** is an associative unital complex algebra $A$ together with a direct-sum grading $A=A_{\bar0}\oplus A_{\bar1}$ for which $A_{\bar i}A_{\bar j}\subseteq A_{\overline{i+j}}$. Its unit belongs to $A_{\bar0}$. Elements of one graded summand are homogeneous, with parity $|a|\in\{0,1\}$. Multiplication is complex-bilinear and associative. A homomorphism of associative superalgebras is a unital algebra homomorphism preserving the grading.

The **supercommutator** of homogeneous $a,b\in A$ is $[a,b]_s:=ab-(-1)^{|a||b|}ba$. This notation is used only for the commutator induced by an associative superalgebra; a general Lie-superalgebra bracket is denoted $[a,b]$.

Left, right and two-sided ideals.

Let $R$ be a ring. An additive subgroup $I\le(R,+)$ is a **left ideal** when
$r i\in I$ for every $r\in R$ and $i\in I$, and a **right ideal** when
$i r\in I$ for every such $r,i$.  A **two-sided ideal**, written
$I\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}R$, is both a left and a right ideal.  In a
commutative ring these three notions agree.

The ideal generated by a subset and principal ideals.

For $S\subseteq R$, define $(S)$ to be the intersection of all two-sided ideals
of $R$ containing $S$.  This family is nonempty because it contains $R$, and
[[lem-ideal-criterion-and-intersections]] shows that $(S)$ is an ideal.  For
$a\in R$, the ideal $(\{a\})$ is written $(a)$ and is called **principal**.

Ideal criteria and intersections of ideals.

A nonempty subset $I\subseteq R$ is a two-sided ideal exactly when it is closed
under $x-y$ and under $rx,xr$ for all $r\in R$, $x,y\in I$.  Any intersection
of two-sided ideals is a two-sided ideal, with the empty intersection equal to
$R$.

Concatenating sums and replacing $a_k$ by $-a_k$ show that $J$ is an additive subgroup; multiplying a sum on the left or right absorbs that factor into $a_k$ or $b_k$, using associativity from [F1], so [F2] makes $J$ a two-sided ideal. It contains every $s\in S$ as $1s1$. Every two-sided ideal containing $S$ contains each $a_k s_k b_k$ and every such finite sum. Thus $J$ is the smallest two-sided ideal containing $S$, and [F3] gives $I=J$.

For each summand $asb$ in a finite expression defining $J$, write $a=a_{\bar0}+a_{\bar1}$ and $b=b_{\bar0}+b_{\bar1}$. Then $asb=\sum_{i,j\in\{0,1\}}a_{\bar i}s b_{\bar j}$; each term is homogeneous by [F1] and lies in $J$. Therefore every homogeneous component of every element of $J$ lies in $J$, proving $I=(I\cap A_{\bar0})\oplus(I\cap A_{\bar1})$. Every coset in $A/I$ decomposes into its even and odd component classes; if a class lies in their intersection, its two homogeneous representatives differ by an element of the graded ideal $I$, so both representatives lie in $I$ and the class is zero. $$ \mathfrak g=\mathfrak g_{\bar 0}\oplus\mathfrak g_{\bar 1} $$
and a complex-bilinear bracket $[\ ,\ ]:\mathfrak g\times\mathfrak g\to\mathfrak g$ satisfying the following conditions. A vector in one summand is **homogeneous**; its **parity** $|x|\in\{0,1\}$ is defined by $x\in\mathfrak g_{\bar{|x|}}$. For homogeneous $x,y,z$:

1. The bracket is graded: $[\mathfrak g_{\bar i},\mathfrak g_{\bar j}]\subseteq\mathfrak g_{\overline{i+j}}$.
2. It is graded-skew: $[x,y]=-(-1)^{|x||y|}[y,x]$.
3. It satisfies the signed Jacobi identity in derivation form:
   $$ [x,[y,z]]=\left\lbrack [x,y],z\right\rbrack+(-1)^{|x||y|}[y,[x,z]]. $$
4. The odd self-Jacobi identity $[x,[x,x]]=0$ for odd $x$ is listed explicitly as part of this convention. Over $\mathbb C$ it follows from condition 3.

All matrix spaces below carry the commutator bracket $[A,B]=AB-BA$ and are
Lie subalgebras of $\mathfrak{gl}_m(\mathbb C)=M_m(\mathbb C)$ in the sense of
[[def-lie-algebra-over-a-field]]; closure under the bracket is verified in
each case by the computation displayed.

* The **general linear Lie algebra** $\mathfrak{gl}_n(\mathbb C)=M_n(\mathbb C)$,
  for $n\ge1$. The **special linear Lie algebra**
  $\mathfrak{sl}_n(\mathbb C)=\{A\in M_n(\mathbb C):\operatorname{tr}A=0\}$
  is a Lie subalgebra because $\operatorname{tr}(AB-BA)=0$, and
  $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$ agrees with
  [[def-special-linear-lie-algebra-sl-two]].
* The **symplectic Lie algebra** $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ is the set of
  $A\in M_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ with $AJ+JA^{T}=0$, for $n\ge1$, where
  $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_n\\-I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$.
* The **orthogonal Lie algebras** $\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ and
  $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$ are the sets of $A\in M_m(\mathbb C)$ with
  $AJ+JA^{T}=0$, for $n\ge1$, where $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_n\\I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$ for
  $m=2n$ and
  $J=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&0&I_n\\0&I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$ for $m=2n+1$.

Solving $AJ+JA^{T}=0$ blockwise gives
$A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&-a^{T}\end{pmatrix}$ for the symplectic and even
orthogonal cases, with $b,c$ symmetric for $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ and
$b,c$ skew-symmetric for $\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$, and gives
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}0&u&-w^{T}\\ w&a&b\\ -u^{T}&c&-a^{T}\end{pmatrix},\qquad u\in M_{1\times n}(\mathbb C),\quad w\in M_{n\times1}(\mathbb C),\quad b,c\ \text{skew-symmetric},$$
for $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$. In particular
$\dim\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)=n(2n+1)=\dim\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$
and $\dim\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)=n(2n-1)$. Each set is closed under the
bracket: if $AJ=-JA^{T}$ and $BJ=-JB^{T}$, then
$[A,B]J+J[A,B]^{T}=ABJ-BAJ+JB^{T}A^{T}-JA^{T}B^{T}$, and substituting
$AJ=-JA^{T}$ and $BJ=-JB^{T}$ (equivalently $JA^{T}=-AJ$ and $JB^{T}=-BJ$) makes
the four terms cancel in pairs. For $n\ge1$, each symplectic or orthogonal family is a nonzero proper subspace of
$M_m(\mathbb C)$ closed under the commutator, hence a Lie subalgebra.

Let $S_+=\mathbb C^2$, $S_-=(\mathbb C^2)^*$, where the algebraic dual is defined in [[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]], and set $V=S_+\otimes_{\mathbb C}S_-$. By [[lem-field-is-a-commutative-ring]], $\mathbb C$ is a commutative ring; use the scalar actions to regard $S_+$ as a right module and $S_-$ as a left module. Use their module tensor product from [[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]; its universal property is [[thm-universal-property-of-module-tensor-products]], and its unique $\mathbb C$-module structure is given by [[thm-commutative-ring-module-structure-on-a-tensor-product]]. Thus $V$ is a complex vector space, every tensor is a finite sum of elementary tensors, and bilinear formulas on $S_+\times S_-$ descend to linear maps on $V$.

Let

Using the standard basis of $S_+$, both summands are copies of $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$, the traceless complex matrix Lie algebra with commutator from [[def-classical-complex-matrix-lie-algebras]].

$$ (A,B)\cdot(u\otimes\phi)=Au\otimes\phi-u\otimes\phi B. $$

$$ [(L,v),(L',v')]=([L,L'],L\cdot v'-L'\cdot v), $$

Let $R$ be a unital ring, $M$ a right $R$-module, $N$ a left $R$-module, and

$$\tau:M\times N\longrightarrow M\otimes_RN,\qquad \tau(m,n)=m\otimes n.$$

The map $\tau$ is balanced ([[def-balanced-and-bilinear-maps]]). For every abelian group $A$ and every balanced map $b:M\times N\to A$, there is a unique group homomorphism

$$\overline b:M\otimes_RN\longrightarrow A$$

such that $\overline b(m\otimes n)=b(m,n)$ for all $m,n$. Consequently composition with $\tau$ is a bijection

$$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Ab}}(M\otimes_RN,A)\cong\operatorname{Bal}_R(M,N;A).$$

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $M,N$ be $R$-modules. The abelian group $M\otimes_RN$ has a unique $R$-module structure for which

$$r(m\otimes n)=(rm)\otimes n=m\otimes(rn)$$

for every $r\in R$, $m\in M$, and $n\in N$.

Let $R$ be a unital ring, $M$ a right $R$-module, and $N$ a left $R$-module. Let

$$F:=\mathbb Z^{(M\times N)}$$

be the free $\mathbb Z$-module on the set $M\times N$ ([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]], [[thm-universal-property-of-free-modules]]), and write $e_{(m,n)}$ for its standard basis elements. The additive group of $F$ is abelian. Let $H$ be the subgroup generated ([[def-generated-subgroup]]) by all elements

$$e_{(m+m',n)}-e_{(m,n)}-e_{(m',n)},$$

$$e_{(m,n+n')}-e_{(m,n)}-e_{(m,n')},$$

and

$$e_{(mr,n)}-e_{(m,rn)}$$

as $m,m'$ range over $M$, $n,n'$ over $N$, and $r$ over $R$. Since every subgroup of an abelian group is normal, the quotient group $F/H$ is defined ([[def-quotient-group]]). The **tensor product of $M$ and $N$ over $R$** is

$$M\otimes_RN:=F/H.$$

The coset of $e_{(m,n)}$ is the **elementary tensor** $m\otimes n$. Every tensor is a finite sum of elementary tensors, because every element of $F$ is a finite $\mathbb Z$-linear combination of basis elements and integer coefficients may be absorbed into either additive variable. The defining relations give

$$(m+m')\otimes n=m\otimes n+m'\otimes n,\qquad m\otimes(n+n')=m\otimes n+m\otimes n',$$

and

$$(mr)\otimes n=m\otimes(rn).$$

In particular $0\otimes n=0=m\otimes0$. No $R$-module structure on $M\otimes_RN$ is part of this arbitrary-ring definition; at this stage it is an abelian group.

Let $F$ be a field ([[def-field]]), with addition $+$, multiplication $\cdot$,
and distinguished elements $0 \ne 1$. Then

1. $(F, +, \cdot, 0, 1)$ is a ring ([[def-ring]]), and it is commutative
   ([[def-commutative-ring]]), with $1 \ne 0$;
2. $F$ is an integral domain ([[def-zero-divisor-and-integral-domain]]);
3. $F$ is a division ring ([[def-division-ring]]), and hence a commutative
   division ring.

The field structure is not changed by this: the ring operations are the field
operations, and the ring's zero and identity are the field's $0$ and $1$.

with $[h_i,h_j]=[e,e]=[f,f]=0$; all reversed even–odd brackets are determined by graded skew symmetry. Denote this bracketed graded vector space by the **gl(1|1) bracket data**. A **complex Lie superalgebra** is a complex vector space $\mathfrak g$ with a specified direct-sum grading
$$ \mathfrak g=\mathfrak g_{\bar 0}\oplus\mathfrak g_{\bar 1} $$
and a complex-bilinear bracket $[\ ,\ ]:\mathfrak g\times\mathfrak g\to\mathfrak g$ satisfying the following conditions. A vector in one summand is **homogeneous**; its **parity** $|x|\in\{0,1\}$ is defined by $x\in\mathfrak g_{\bar{|x|}}$. For homogeneous $x,y,z$:

2. It is graded-skew: $[x,y]=-(-1)^{|x||y|}[y,x]$.
3. It satisfies the signed Jacobi identity in derivation form:
   $$ [x,[y,z]]=\left\lbrack [x,y],z\right\rbrack+(-1)^{|x||y|}[y,[x,z]]. $$

If $p_i$ is the projection onto $V_{\bar i}$, every $T\in\operatorname{End}(V)$ decomposes uniquely as $T_0+T_1$, where $T_0=p_0Tp_0+p_1Tp_1$ and $T_1=p_1Tp_0+p_0Tp_1$; hence these spaces give a direct-sum grading. Composition sends parities $i,j$ to $i+j$ because an operator of parity $j$ maps $V_{\bar k}$ into $V_{\overline{k+j}}$, and the identity is even. Composition is associative and complex-bilinear, so by [F4] this makes $\operatorname{End}(V)$ a unital associative superalgebra. Given a $\mathfrak g$-supermodule, each homogeneous $x$ acts as a parity-$|x|$ endomorphism $v\mapsto x\cdot v$. The module identity in [F1] says exactly that this map preserves the Lie bracket into the endomorphism supercommutator, so [F3] extends it uniquely to a unital graded algebra action of $U(\mathfrak g)$.

Conversely, restrict a unital graded left $U(\mathfrak g)$-module action along $\iota_{\mathfrak g}$. Applying the quotient relation [F2] to $v$ gives $[x,y]v=x(yv)-(-1)^{|x||y|}y(xv)$; grading and bilinearity are inherited from the module action. Thus the restriction is a $\mathfrak g$-supermodule.

Starting from a supermodule, the extension in [F3] restricts to the original action by its defining property. Starting from a $U(\mathfrak g)$-module, the extension of its restriction agrees with the original action on every generator $\iota_{\mathfrak g}(x)$ and on the unit; these generate the quotient algebra by [F2], so the actions agree on all of $U(\mathfrak g)$.

A parity-preserving linear map intertwines the $\mathfrak g$-actions exactly when it intertwines the restrictions of the $U(\mathfrak g)$-actions: one direction is restriction, and the other follows on products of generators and then on finite linear combinations. The correspondence is therefore mutually inverse on objects and morphisms.

with $[h_i,h_j]=[e,e]=[f,f]=0$; all reversed even–odd brackets are determined by graded skew symmetry. Denote this bracketed graded vector space by the **gl(1|1) bracket data**. The next item proves that it is a Lie superalgebra; until then this definition is only the specified vector space and bracket table.

Let $\mathfrak g$ be a complex Lie superalgebra. A **left $\mathfrak g$-supermodule** is a complex vector space with grading $V=V_{\bar0}\oplus V_{\bar1}$ and a complex-bilinear action $\mathfrak g\times V\to V$, denoted $(x,v)\mapsto x\cdot v$, such that $\mathfrak g_{\bar i}\cdot V_{\bar j}\subseteq V_{\overline{i+j}}$ and, for homogeneous $x,y\in\mathfrak g$,
$$ [x,y]\cdot v=x\cdot(y\cdot v)-(-1)^{|x||y|}y\cdot(x\cdot v)\qquad(v\in V). $$
A **parity-preserving homomorphism** of supermodules is a complex-linear map $T:V\to W$ preserving the two graded summands and satisfying $T(x\cdot v)=x\cdot T(v)$. A **representation** is the same action data written as an even linear map $\rho:\mathfrak g\to\operatorname{End}(V)$, where an endomorphism has parity $i$ when it maps $V_{\bar j}$ to $V_{\overline{i+j}}$; composition gives the supercommutator from [[def-associative-superalgebra-over-complex-numbers]].

Fix a triangular decomposition datum $(\mathfrak n^-,\mathfrak h,\mathfrak n^+)$ as in [[def-triangular-decomposition-of-a-lie-superalgebra]] and a left $\mathfrak g$-supermodule $V$. Here $\mathfrak h^*=\mathcal L(\mathfrak h,\mathbb C)$ is the algebraic dual from [[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]. $$ h\cdot v=\lambda(h)v\quad(h\in\mathfrak h),\qquad n\cdot v=0\quad(n\in\mathfrak n^+). $$
The **highest-weight module generated by** $v$ is the smallest graded $\mathfrak g$-invariant subspace containing $v$, equivalently the span of $v$ and all vectors $x_1\cdots x_r\cdot v$ with $r\ge1$ and homogeneous $x_i\in\mathfrak g$. A **unital associative superalgebra over $\mathbb C$** is an associative unital complex algebra $A$ together with a direct-sum grading $A=A_{\bar0}\oplus A_{\bar1}$ for which $A_{\bar i}A_{\bar j}\subseteq A_{\overline{i+j}}$. Its unit belongs to $A_{\bar0}$. Elements of one graded summand are homogeneous, with parity $|a|\in\{0,1\}$. Multiplication is complex-bilinear and associative. A homomorphism of associative superalgebras is a unital algebra homomorphism preserving the grading.

The **supercommutator** of homogeneous $a,b\in A$ is $[a,b]_s:=ab-(-1)^{|a||b|}ba$. This notation is used only for the commutator induced by an associative superalgebra; a general Lie-superalgebra bracket is denoted $[a,b]$.

Equivalently, the canonical map $R^{(I\times J)}\to M\otimes_RN$ sending the standard basis vector at $(i,j)$ to $e_i\otimes f_j$ is an isomorphism. This includes an empty basis in either factor.

Let $V$ be a vector space over $F$. A **linear functional** on $V$ is a linear map $f:V\to F$, where $F$ is regarded as a vector space over itself. The **algebraic dual space** of $V$ is

$$V^*:=\mathcal L(V,F),$$

with pointwise addition and scalar multiplication. This is the full algebraic dual: no topology, norm, or continuity condition is imposed.

Let $F$ be a field ([[def-field]]), with addition $+$, multiplication $\cdot$,
and distinguished elements $0 \ne 1$. Then

1. $(F, +, \cdot, 0, 1)$ is a ring ([[def-ring]]), and it is commutative
   ([[def-commutative-ring]]), with $1 \ne 0$;
2. $F$ is an integral domain ([[def-zero-divisor-and-integral-domain]]);
3. $F$ is a division ring ([[def-division-ring]]), and hence a commutative
   division ring.

The field structure is not changed by this: the ring operations are the field
operations, and the ring's zero and identity are the field's $0$ and $1$.
